Here human-machine collaboration is genuinely reciprocal, and originality, coherence, and expressive intent form the evaluation criteria. Each stage also hands something forward, since the artefact and the competence produced at one stage become the entry condition for the next: a student who has already interrogated a script arrives at modelling with a plan rather than a blank scene. The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Screening data were not analyzed as a separate strand, did not generate hypotheses for the case analysis, and were not merged with the qualitative findings; they were used only to locate each focal case within the cohort distribution ( Table 1 ). The primary purpose of the case study was explanatory: to examine how epistemic authority shifted during AI-assisted lesson planning and what enabled those shifts. Each participant constituted a case. Cases were embedded, with individual planning episodes serving as subunits of analysis within each case. Focal cases and preliminary screening context. The study took place in a required undergraduate course, Study of Elementary Mathematics , within the third year of a four-year preservice mathematics teacher education program at a pseudonymized Chinese university (“Y University”). Y University was selected as the study site because members of the research team were faculty members there, which provided access to the program and familiarity with its curriculum. The focal task was completed after regular class hours on 17 March 2026 and did not count toward course assessment. Following identification during the preliminary quantitative screening, selected participants were invited to complete the task voluntarily. The task was completed within a suggested 45-min window. Participants could finish early or continue until they judged the plan complete. Researchers observed the task in person and additionally reviewed screen recordings retrospectively. Participants worked individually with an AI interface beside a Microsoft Word document and were asked to create a complete mathematics lesson plan. No template was imposed, and completeness was self-determined by each participant. They were instructed to select a junior-secondary topic. Suggested topics were slope, side-angle-side (SAS) triangle congruence proof, operations with negative numbers, and solving one-variable linear equations, although they could propose another topic. Participants could use any publicly accessible AI chat interface of their choosing. They also chose their own initial and subsequent prompts. Three participants used Doubao (ByteDance) and two used DeepSeek, all through the free public web interfaces on 17 March 2026. The deep-thinking function was enabled in T3’s session and the web-search function in T2’s session; neither function was enabled in the other sessions. No model version was recorded. As these interfaces are updated over time, the AI outputs analyzed here reflect the versions available on that date. All prompts submitted during the task are listed in Supplementary Table S1 . AI responses were not archived as text; they are visible in the screen recordings and are summarized for each episode in the evidence matrix ( Supplementary Table S2 ). Concurrent verbalization was encouraged to capture reactions and small decisions, but continuous think-aloud talk was not mandatory. The screening dataset contained complete records of questionnaire and performance tasks for 42 preservice mathematics teachers. The questionnaire was developed by the research team for this study. The four dimensions correspond to constructs discussed in research on AI literacy, epistemic vigilance, reliance on automation, cognitive offloading, achievement goal orientation, and epistemic agency ( Ames, 1992 ; Damsa et al., 2010 ; Long and Magerko, 2020 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ; Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Sperber et al., 2010 ). The composite used for case selection drew on 20 five-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) representing four dimensions each, with five items: critical evaluation of AI output (A1), AI dependence (A2), performative orientation (A3), and active reconstruction (A4). Before administration, the items were reviewed by a second researcher, who had not been involved in drafting them, for clarity and correspondence to their intended dimensions. Representative items include “I can judge whether the definitions or reasoning steps given by AI contain logical gaps” (A1), “I usually adopt AI-generated lesson-plan structures directly, without making any adjustments” (A2), “When designing a lesson plan, I give priority to whether it looks professional rather than whether I fully understand the content” (A3), and “I treat AI output as raw material and creatively reconstruct it rather than using it directly” (A4). Because the composite combined conceptually distinct dimensions, reliability was examined separately for each dimension. Each of the five participants retained, shared, or ceded authority in different decisions, and no participant could be described by a single position ( Table 2 ). Across the 34 decision episodes, authority was retained in 16, shared in 12, and ceded in 6. As decisions differed in scope and importance, the counts indicate where evidence is located rather than how agentic each participant was, and they are not used to rank participants ( Table 2 ). Descriptive distribution of authority positions. The analysis identified three recurring patterns. First, complete AI-generated plans shifted plans by changing the starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, the most frequent visible actions did not correspond to a single authority position, and an articulated professional warrant was not always enacted in the plan. Third, when participants were uncertain, authority tended to shift toward the AI, unless they could draw on professional resources, such as knowledge of student thinking or practicum experience. T1 began by asking Doubao for a Grade 8 lesson on the properties of parallelograms. The screen recording shows that she scrolled through the entire response once, then selected it all and pasted it into Word. In her written reflection, she explained: “I thought there was no major problem with the overall framework, but I was not very sure that it was a good design, so I accepted it”. The AI plan became the default trajectory before she had articulated a mathematical or pedagogical criterion. This episode was coded as ceding authority. T1’s later decisions, however, showed a different pattern. After reviewing the plan she pasted, she noticed that it did not address how students might respond during the activities or how the teacher should respond in turn. She entered a follow-up prompt: “You overlooked anticipated student responses and response strategies in your design”. Drawing on the content that Doubao then generated, she added anticipated student responses and response strategies to the activities in her Word document. This decision was coded as shared: T1 identified the gap and selected what to include, but the AI supplied most of the substantive content. However, for the proof of the second property, T1 did not rely on the AI’s content. The AI’s plan presented complete teacher demonstrations of both proofs. T1 reorganized this sequence so that the teacher would model the first proof, after which students would attempt the second proof themselves by drawing on the first. She typed a new teacher–student activity directly into the Word document: “The teacher asks students to discuss in groups how to prove the property, and invites a student to write the proof on the board”. For this activity, she did not adopt the anticipated responses that Doubao had generated. Instead, she wrote her own: “Students have gained experience from the previous proof and know that the property can be proved by showing that triangles are congruent.” In the stimulated-recall interview, she explained that after the teacher’s model, students should be able to “draw inferences from one case to another.” This interview account was consistent with the anticipated response she had outlined during planning. The reconstruction was coded as retained. The shift, therefore, was not from using AI to not using it. Rather, it was a shift from accepting an entire plan because it appeared coherent to redesigning part of it based on how students might reason. T3 began from the opposite position. Before prompting DeepSeek, he divided the lesson into four modules: objectives, key and difficult points, materials, and lesson content. His reflection explained: “If I have my own framework first, I can keep adjusting it”. He then asked the AI to fill these modules one at a time. For example, he first requested objectives for a lesson on SAS triangle congruence, then asked the AI to shorten and summarize them, and only after settling the objectives and key points did he ask for a sequence of lesson activities based on them. This teacher-authored structure determined what the AI was asked to generate and in what order, and it was coded as retained. Within this structure, most of T3’s subsequent decisions involved working with AI-generated content rather than replacing it. He asked the AI to anticipate students’ possible answers and simulate the classroom interaction for the introduction. For the “standard proof writing” segment, he asked the AI what students should pay particular attention to when writing proofs. Then he used its answer to add notes on format, the correspondence of conditions, and the completeness of conditions. In some places, however, he contributed content of his own. For the AI-generated variation exercises, he used a mathematical drawing tool to create figures that matched each problem’s conditions. The framework did not guarantee continued control. When he reached the “hands-on exploration” segment late in the session, the screen recording shows he hesitated for a long time before engaging with the AI-generated activity. In his recall interview, he explained that time was running short and that he did not know how to design the activity himself. No independent mathematical or pedagogical warrant for the activity appeared in any source, and the decision was therefore coded as ceded under the first criterion. His reflection suggested an awareness of this risk: accepting the AI’s wording, he wrote, could lead him to “gradually enter its rhythm”. T3’s case thus shows that a teacher-authored framework can support authority over the overall structure of a lesson without preventing local shifts back toward the AI. These cases address RQ1 in two ways. First, T1’s case shows that a complete AI-generated plan can change a novice’s starting task from constructing a lesson to deciding whether to accept one. Second, neither case settled into a stable position of authority. T1 later reclaimed authority by redesigning part of the plan, whereas T3, who began with his own framework, later adopted AI-generated content without a visible warrant. Authority thus shifted in both directions over the course of a single planning session. Across all five cases, this movement exhibited a temporal pattern: two of the six ceded episodes were the first episode of a case (T1, T5), in which a complete AI plan was adopted, and the remaining four occurred later in the planning session. analysis.discussion: The first contribution of this study concerns how GenAI changes the starting conditions of learning to plan. A complete AI plan did not simply supply ideas. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. This finding adds to existing research on preservice teachers and GenAI. Previous studies have mainly examined preservice teachers’ AI-related knowledge (AI-TPACK), their perceptions of the benefits of GenAI, and their integration of it into lesson planning ( Aldemir et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Kılıçkaya and Kic-Drgas, 2025 ). These aspects remain important, but they do not show which instructional decisions preservice teachers actually make for themselves when AI is involved. Nor does visible human participation guarantee the kind of hybrid intelligence envisioned in human-AI collaboration ( Cukurova, 2025 ). The present cases show that participation in the process alone is not enough to meet this condition. These cases point to a more demanding standard: preservice teachers should be able to identify, warrant, and assume responsibility for consequential instructional decisions. The finding also contributes to practice-based teacher education. Approximations are valuable when they preserve the core work novices need to learn ( Grossman et al., 2009 ). Simulation-based environments similarly create protected opportunities to rehearse decisions and examine their consequences ( Dieker et al., 2014 ; Ke and Xu, 2020 ). We propose that AI-assisted planning is more likely to remain an approximation of practice when the task requires preservice teachers to decompose the problem, anticipate students, compare alternatives, and justify transformations. A task that simply asks for a complete lesson plan may allow the AI to do much of this work. A task that asks preservice teachers to examine an AI plan and revise it against explicit professional criteria is more likely to help them retain this work. The second contribution is a decision-level account of professional judgment in lesson planning. The findings show that judgment could not be inferred from the amount of prompting or editing because the same visible action carried different meanings across episodes. Prompting the AI could keep authority with the participant or leave the AI as the substantive source. Retaining an AI proposal could follow deliberate comparison or unexamined trust. Recognizing a missing response could demonstrate pedagogical awareness while leaving AI’s plan unchanged. As warrant and enactment are part of how authority was defined, the substantive finding is that neither the type nor the amount of visible activity tracked these criteria. This finding brings research on epistemic agency into direct contact with professional judgment and professional noticing. Epistemic agency has emphasized responsibility for knowledge advancement and the negotiation of what counts as legitimate knowledge ( Damsa et al., 2010 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Stroupe, 2014 ). In lesson planning, the knowledge object is prospective practice. Responsibility is therefore visible when a teacher’s mathematical, curricular, pedagogical, or feasibility judgment changes what students would encounter. This interpretation is consistent with accounts of teacher judgment and noticing in which teachers attend to consequential information, interpret it through professional knowledge, and connect it to action ( Shulman, 1987 ; van Es and Sherin, 2008 ; Jacobs et al., 2010 ). The source-action-warrant-enactment sequence offers a way to observe that responsibility without treating AI contribution as inherently displacing or teacher editing as inherently agentic. The decision-level analysis also qualifies participant typologies. Song et al. (2025) identified useful patterns and levels in teachers’ GenAI integration, but the present cases show that professional authority can vary across different objects within the same planning session. T1 both ceded and retained authority; T4 both enacted a student-oriented sequencing decision and left other pedagogical insights outside the plan. Typologies may summarize broad orientations, but they should not be assumed to describe every professional decision. In these cases, ecological agency offered a more plausible account of this variation than a stable user trait ( Priestley et al., 2015 ). In the present cases, knowledge of student thinking, practicum experience, mathematical structure, and judgment about lesson capacity enabled authority to remain with the preservice teacher. Uncertainty about content or curriculum, limited teaching experience, and the fluent completeness of AI output made independent evaluation more difficult. Authority therefore had to be re-established for each consequential decision rather than secured once for the whole task. The third contribution is methodological: claims about professional judgment require evidence of how decisions developed. In this study, the screen recordings established what participants did and in what order, while the interviews and reflections supplied, extended, or complicated their reasons. Together, these sources revealed two vulnerabilities that would have been difficult to identify from final plans alone. The two differ in empirical breadth.
